prompt: What does the elements panel show that viewing the source does not?
hint: One is what was sent.

choices.text: The tree as it exists now, repairs and script changes included
choices.why: Which is the whole reason to use it rather than the file.

choices.text: The file after compression, which is what the browser received
choices.why: The source shows the decompressed text; nothing here is about compression.

choices.text: The markup with the comments removed, which is what the browser keeps
choices.why: Comments are kept in the document; removal is not what differs.

choices.text: The styles, which the source shows as a link to a file rather than as the rules themselves
choices.why: True, and a consequence rather than the difference being asked about.

prompt: A rule you expected is shown struck through. What does that mean?
hint: The panel is showing the cascade.

choices.text: The rule is in a stylesheet that failed to load, so no rule applied
choices.why: A rule from a file that did not load would not be listed at all.

choices.text: Something more specific, or later, won for that property
choices.why: The cascade of lesson ten, with the losers visible.

choices.text: The rule has a syntax error, which the browser struck out while parsing
choices.why: An invalid declaration is shown differently, usually with a warning marker.

choices.text: The element is hidden, so the browser marks its styles as inactive
choices.why: Hidden elements show their styles normally.

prompt: Fill the blank: when a thing sits 17 pixels from the left and nobody can say why, the ___ tab shows the final value of every property rather than the rules.
hint: It is the answer, not the argument.

prompt: Which of these are true of editing a value in this panel? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two of them are the reason it is safe.

choices.text: The page updates as you type
choices.why: Which is what makes it a good place to experiment.

choices.text: A reload discards everything you changed
choices.why: Nothing is saved, which is exactly the safety.

choices.text: It does not reach your files
choices.why: Obvious written down, and the source of the occasional lost hour.

choices.text: It changes what other visitors see
choices.why: It changes this window and nothing beyond it.

choices.text: It is written to the stylesheet the rule came from
choices.why: Nothing is written anywhere.

prompt: Why is forcing an element into a hover state worth knowing about?
hint: Some things vanish when you move the pointer.

choices.text: It triggers the event listeners attached to the element
choices.why: It sets the state for styling; listeners are a separate tab.

choices.text: It shows what the rule would do on a device without a pointer
choices.why: A useful question, and not what this control answers.

choices.text: It keeps a menu open for inspection
choices.why: The one people do not discover alone and then use daily.

choices.text: It applies the hover rule permanently, which is how a design is tested
choices.why: It is a temporary state like everything else here.

prompt: You open a page, then open the network panel, and the list is empty. Why?
hint: It records from a particular moment.

choices.text: A filter is hiding everything, since the default filter shows failures alone
choices.why: The default filter shows everything.

choices.text: The page finished before the panel could attach, which a slower connection would fix
choices.why: Attaching is not a race; the panel simply was not recording.

choices.text: The requests were all answered from the cache, so no rows were created
choices.why: Cache hits appear as rows saying so, which is one of the panel's uses.

choices.text: The panel records only while it is open
choices.why: Open it first, then reload — the smallest possible habit.

prompt: Match each column to what it tells you.
hint: One of them says a request never left the machine.

pairs.right: The three digits, and whose fault they name
What came over the wire, or that nothing did
The whole duration of that one request
What the response said the bytes were

right_distractors: How many times it has been requested today

prompt: Which sort finds the single most common performance defect in the world?
hint: Something nobody meant to publish.

choices.text: By size
choices.why: The four-megabyte image, found in about a second.

choices.text: By status, which groups the failures together at one end
choices.why: Useful, and failures are not usually a performance defect.

choices.text: By type, which puts the scripts beside each other
choices.why: Helpful for reading, and it does not rank anything.

choices.text: By name, which puts files from the same folder together
choices.why: Tidy, and it tells you nothing about cost.

prompt: Fill the blank: turning on ___ log keeps the rows across a navigation, so a redirect or a form submission does not wipe the evidence.
hint: One word, and it is the opposite of discarding.

prompt: A colleague measures the site with the cache disabled and reports a number. What is wrong with it?
hint: Ask who experiences that.

choices.text: It is valid just when throttling is also on, which pairs with it
choices.why: They are independent settings and neither requires the other.

choices.text: It is the number for a first visit, which is not what most visitors have
choices.why: A site measured that way is a site nobody actually loads.

choices.text: It is optimistic, because disabling the cache removes the time spent checking copies
choices.why: It is pessimistic: everything is fetched rather than served from disk.

choices.text: It is unusable, because the setting also turns off compression
choices.why: It affects neither compression nor anything else about the transfer.

prompt: A button does nothing and there is a red line in the console. What is the most likely relationship?
hint: Something stopped happening.

choices.text: The error is a warning about a deprecated feature, which does not stop anything
choices.why: A warning is not an error, and the question says a red line.

choices.text: The red line is from a third-party script and is unrelated to the button
choices.why: Possible, and the first assumption should be the cheaper one to check.

choices.text: They are very likely the same fact
choices.why: Something threw, and what it was doing stopped.

choices.text: The console reports the button's click, so the line is the click being recorded
choices.why: A click is not logged unless somebody logged it.

prompt: An error points at line 1, column 40000. What is missing?
hint: The file was built rather than written.

choices.text: A newline, which the build should have kept so that lines stay meaningful
choices.why: Removing them is the point of the build; the map is what recovers the meaning.

choices.text: The stack, which is collapsed by default and holds the real position
choices.why: The stack has the same unhelpful positions in it.

choices.text: The original file, which has to be deployed beside the built one
choices.why: Close, and what is deployed is a map rather than the original.

choices.text: A source map
choices.why: It maps the built code back to what was written, and the browser loads it automatically.

prompt: Somebody asks you to paste a line into the console of a site you are signed in to. What is happening?
hint: Large sites print a warning about exactly this.

choices.text: That is the attack
choices.why: The line runs with the authority of the page, and sends the session elsewhere.

choices.text: A support technique, which is why browsers permit pasting
choices.why: Pasting exists for your own work rather than for somebody else's instructions.

choices.text: A test of the site's security, which will be refused by the browser
choices.why: The browser refuses nothing; it is your own console.

choices.text: A common way of reporting a bug, and the line collects diagnostic information
choices.why: Nobody needs your session to collect diagnostics.

prompt: Fill the blank: in the console, `___` refers to whatever element is currently selected in the elements panel.
hint: A dollar and a digit.

prompt: A form reports success, nothing was saved, and the console is completely clean. What does the clean console tell you?
hint: It is information, and a narrow kind.

choices.text: That the failure is on the server rather than in the page's code
choices.why: Close, and a clean console does not establish where the failure was.

choices.text: That nothing threw, and nothing more
choices.why: A `200` with an error in the body produces a perfectly clean console.

choices.text: That the request never left the browser, since a failure would have been reported
choices.why: Backwards: a request that failed to leave would be reported here.

choices.text: That the page's code caught the error and handled it quietly
choices.why: Possible, and the clean console is equally consistent with nothing having gone wrong in it.

prompt: Match each bar to what it tells you to fix.
hint: Each one points at a different person.

pairs.right: The file: compress it, resize it, send less
Too many hosts, or a server far away
A cold lookup, in front of everything else

right_distractors: The number of rules in the stylesheet

prompt: A request took 5.4 seconds, of which 5.2 was the waiting bar. What does that rule out?
hint: One bar belongs to the server alone.

choices.text: A slow name lookup, which would appear inside the waiting bar
choices.why: DNS has a bar of its own, in front of this one.

choices.text: The protocol version, which decides how requests are queued
choices.why: That affects the queued bar rather than the waiting one.

choices.text: Compressing the response, which would shorten the download and not the wait
choices.why: No CDN, no smaller image and no compression touches that bar.

choices.text: A slow database query, since waiting covers the network as well
choices.why: Waiting is precisely the server thinking, and a query is inside it.

prompt: The waterfall shows a staircase — each request starting as the previous one finishes. What does that suggest?
hint: Things are being discovered one at a time.

choices.text: The server is refusing concurrent requests from one address
choices.why: Servers rarely do that, and the browser's own limits come first.

choices.text: The panel is sorting by start time, which produces this shape on any page
choices.why: A page with parallel requests shows a wall in the same sorting.

choices.text: The connection is slow, so requests are being sent one after another
choices.why: A slow connection makes bars longer rather than sequential.

choices.text: A serial chain: something is discovered only after the thing before it arrives
choices.why: A stylesheet importing a stylesheet, a script fetching a script, a chain of redirects.

prompt: Fill the blank: the bar that is the server thinking, and the one number in the breakdown that belongs to the server alone, is ___.
hint: The request has gone and nothing has come back.

prompt: The network panel goes quiet for a second in the middle of a load, with a wide gap and no rows. What is happening?
hint: Nothing is downloading, and time is passing.

choices.text: The browser is busy: parsing, running a script, or laying out
choices.why: The network panel is quiet and the performance panel is where the time went.

choices.text: The server is holding the connection open without sending anything
choices.why: That shows as a waiting bar on a row rather than as an absence of rows.

choices.text: The panel stopped recording, which happens when a navigation occurs
choices.why: A navigation clears the list unless the log is preserved.

choices.text: A request is queued behind the six-connection limit and has not started
choices.why: A queued request shows as a row with a long first bar.

prompt: A page takes six seconds. One row is 5.5 s and everything else is under 200 ms. What kind of problem is it?
hint: Sort by time and read the top row.

choices.text: A uniformly slow page, which needs a CDN and smaller files throughout
choices.why: Nothing about this page is uniformly slow.

choices.text: One slow thing, and the rest of the page is fine
choices.why: A different problem from a slow page, with nothing in common but the complaint.

choices.text: A slow connection, since one large request is what saturates a link
choices.why: A saturated link would slow the other rows as well.

choices.text: A rendering problem, since the network total is just six seconds
choices.why: Six seconds of one request is a network row, and it is on the screen.

prompt: That 5.5-second row is a script from another host, with no `async`. What is the consequence beyond its own time?
hint: Lesson ten, arriving through somebody else's outage.

choices.text: The page is served without it, since a browser abandons a slow script
choices.why: Nothing abandons it; the wait is what the page experiences.

choices.text: The stylesheet is applied twice, once before and once after it runs
choices.why: Nothing reapplies a stylesheet because of a script.

choices.text: The parser is stopped behind it, so nothing is drawn either
choices.why: One attribute fixes the page, and nothing about the site was wrong.

choices.text: The other requests are queued behind it and start late
choices.why: The preload scanner keeps fetching; it is the tree that waits.

prompt: A form says it saved, nothing was saved, the console is clean and the request shows `200`. Where do you look next?
hint: One panel shows what actually came back.

choices.text: The request headers, to check the cookie was sent
choices.why: Worth a glance, and a missing cookie would usually produce a 401 rather than a 200.

choices.text: The performance panel, since the page is doing something after the response
choices.why: Something is wrong with the answer rather than with the time it took.

choices.text: The elements panel, to see whether the confirmation was inserted into the tree
choices.why: It plainly was, which is why the visitor saw it.

choices.text: The response body of that request
choices.why: An error under a 200, which is lesson six's most expensive mistake.

prompt: Fill the blank: the habit this lesson is really teaching is to ___ before guessing.
hint: Four letters, and it is what the panel is for.

prompt: Which of these are visible in the network panel? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of the five come straight from earlier lessons.

choices.text: A cookie's Secure and HttpOnly attributes
choices.why: In the headers, and as columns in the storage panel.

choices.text: Each hop of a redirect chain, with its own status
choices.why: Three round trips is three rows you can count.

choices.text: Whether a response came from the cache
choices.why: The size column says disk cache or memory cache.

choices.text: Which stylesheet rule won for an element
choices.why: That is the elements panel, and a different question.

choices.text: How long a layout took
choices.why: That is the performance panel; the network is quiet during it.

prompt: A page is fine on your machine and slow for a client in another country. What do you turn on before measuring again?
hint: Your connection is not theirs.

choices.text: Throttling
choices.why: Your machine is fast and in the same city as the server; almost nobody else is.

choices.text: Disable cache, so the measurement is not affected by your own copies
choices.why: That measures a first visit, which is a different distortion rather than a fix.

choices.text: The accessibility tab, which reports what assistive software sees
choices.why: Unrelated to the question being asked.

choices.text: Preserve log, so the rows survive the navigation
choices.why: Useful for a different question entirely.

prompt: Put these in the order the lesson recommends for a page that is misbehaving.
hint: Start with the cheapest thing to check.
items: Open the console: did anything throw?
Open the network panel: what came back, and with which status?
Open the response body: is the answer what it claims to be?
Open the performance panel, if the network was quiet and time still passed
trap: The tempting order starts with the performance panel, because the complaint was about speed. It is last: three cheaper checks come first, and most problems are settled before you reach it.

prompt: A page contacts eleven hosts. Which cost does that impose that a single host would not?
hint: Two bars are paid once per connection.

choices.text: Eleven certificates to verify, which the browser does in series
choices.why: Verification is part of the negotiation and is not the serial cost here.

choices.text: Eleven name lookups and eleven connection negotiations
choices.why: Which is why a page spread across many hosts pays them many times.

choices.text: Eleven times the bandwidth, since each host sends its own copy
choices.why: Each sends different files; the bytes are not multiplied.

choices.text: Eleven separate caches, which are not shared between the hosts
choices.why: True and rarely what costs; the caches hold different things anyway.

prompt: Somebody copies a request as a command line and pastes it into a group chat. What is the problem?
hint: Ask what the command carries.

choices.text: It stops working the moment it is pasted, so it is useless to anybody
choices.why: It works, which is exactly the problem.

choices.text: It reveals the server's address, which was not otherwise public
choices.why: The address is public by definition and is not the sensitive part.

choices.text: It contains the session cookie, which is a working credential in plain text
choices.why: It does not belong in a message, a ticket, or anything that outlives the session.

choices.text: It contains the response, which may hold somebody's personal data
choices.why: The copied command is the request; the response is not in it.

prompt: The DNS bar is large on the first request to a host and absent on the rest. Why?
hint: Lesson eight answered this.

choices.text: The browser reuses the connection, which carries the name with it
choices.why: Connection reuse removes the connecting bar rather than the DNS one.

choices.text: The panel reports it once per host and hides the repeats
choices.why: Nothing is hidden; the later requests genuinely have no lookup.

choices.text: The lookups after the first were sent in parallel, so they cost no time
choices.why: There are no further lookups to send.

choices.text: The answer was cached after the first lookup
choices.why: Which is what the three caches of lesson eight are for.

prompt: Which sentence separates the three numbers properly for somebody who says only *the site is slow*?
hint: Three owners, three numbers.

choices.text: The server answered in 40 ms, the first paint was at 2 s, and the difference is a stylesheet and a blocking script
choices.why: Every part of that comes off one chart, and it is a different conversation.

choices.text: The site takes two seconds, which is above the threshold most visitors tolerate
choices.why: A summary of the complaint rather than a separation of it.

choices.text: The network is slow today, which the throttling setting confirms
choices.why: Throttling simulates a slow network rather than confirming one.

choices.text: The server and the browser are both slow, and each needs its own investigation
choices.why: The whole point of the chart is that it tells you which one.

prompt: What is the honest claim this lesson makes about everything before it?
hint: The course has been describing something.

choices.text: The earlier lessons were simplified, and this one shows the real behaviour
choices.why: Nothing earlier was a simplification of what this panel shows.

choices.text: Every one of those things is visible, on any site, in a panel already installed
choices.why: The requests, the headers, the tree, the milliseconds — the actual ones.

choices.text: The tools replace the need to understand the earlier lessons
choices.why: The panel shows numbers; the lessons are what make them mean something.

choices.text: The panel works only on sites you built, since it needs the source
choices.why: It works on anything, which is how a great deal of this is learned.
